newsitem.title: USA: American Jews concerned about Egyptian media.
newsitem.headline: American Jews concerned about Egyptian media.

text.p: Jewish-American representatives told Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Wednesday they were concerned that some cartoons and commentary in the Egyptian media had taken an anti-Semitic tone.

Mubarak indicated he could not interfere with his country's press but he did not support moves that would instill hatred, said Max Kampelman, an official with the American Jewish Committee, a Jewish human rights group.

"Concern was expressed by the (Jewish) delegation that these cartoons and criticism that have sometimes taken on the nature of anti-Semitism, or anti-Israel, were not the way to proceed in order to instill a spirit of peace," Kampelman told reporters in Washington after he and other Jewish representatives met with Mubarak.
"President Mubarak indicated to us that he did not have the authority to interfere with the Egyptian press in that area, and it was a free press," Kampelman said.

"I don't like to speak for him, but I received certainly the impression that he was not interested in supporting any kind of moves in Egypt which would tend to instill hate or discrimination or distress in any way," Kampelman said.
"He also indicated his view that there probably were in Israel itself severe criticism of him and of Egypt but he understood that also was part of the price you pay for a free press."

Mubarak arrived in Washington last Saturday and held about three hours of talks with President Clinton on Monday. But he received a cool welcome from the Anti-Defamation League, a Jewish group that fights racism.

It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times asking Mubarak to "stop the anti-semitic hate in Egypt." The ad showed Egyptian cartoons of Israeli soldiers carrying flags with the Nazi swastika emblazoned on them.

Middle East peace negotiations have been roiled in recent weeks by several events, including an Israeli decision to build 6,500 housing units in a part of Arab East Jerusalem and its taking steps to close four PLO offices in the city.

Kampelman said American Jews were divided on the development. "I don't think the American Jewish community is in a position to try to express its own unified position when there isn't a unified position on the issue," he said.
He said he was satisfied that Mubarak was committed to peace. "The president made it very clear that he will not change his committment to peace. And we obviously encouraged him in that regard."
